Israel proposes new space law requiring permits for satellite launches, sales, and asteroid mining

The drafted law also addresses legal responsibility for damage caused by space activities, including potential accidents involving satellites and other spacecraft.

Israel's Science and Technology Ministry published a draft Outer Space Law on Thursday, proposing a comprehensive regulatory framework for space activities conducted within Israel and by Israeli citizens and companies operating abroad.

The legislation would require prior government authorization for a range of space-related activities, including launching spacecraft, operating satellites, extracting resources in space, and buying or selling objects in orbit.

The proposed law is intended to establish oversight of Israel's growing space sector while ensuring compliance with international obligations and national security requirements.

Israel's proposed space law would regulate activities beyond its borders

Under the proposed legislation, Israeli citizens and corporations would be subject to national space regulations even when conducting operations outside Israel.

The framework is designed to enable Israel to supervise space activities in accordance with its international commitments, particularly those arising from the Outer Space Treaty and other international agreements.

National security considerations and additional regulatory requirements would also play a role in determining whether space activities receive authorization.

Beyond government oversight, the legislation could provide greater regulatory certainty for Israeli space technology companies.

Israeli companies are periodically required to present government approvals to foreign launch providers and regulators. The proposed law would establish a clearer, more structured process for obtaining such permits.

Satellite launches, asteroid mining, and spacecraft sales would require permits

At the center of the draft legislation is a licensing mechanism requiring operators to obtain advance approval from the director of the Israel Space Agency, which operates under the Science and Technology Ministry.

The proposed definition of "space activity" includes launching spacecraft, controlling the movement of objects in outer space, extracting mineral resources, and purchasing or selling space objects.

Consequently, companies seeking to launch satellites, conduct asteroid mining operations, or transfer ownership of spacecraft would need regulatory approval before proceeding.

The director of the Israel Space Agency would also have authority to make permits conditional on compliance with safety requirements, environmental protection measures, and efforts to reduce space debris.

Israel plans national registry to track satellites and other space objects

The proposed legislation would also establish a national registry of launched space objects.

The registry would record identifying information about each object, including its launch location and date, intended purpose, and orbital trajectory.

Certain information from the registry would be made publicly available, allowing greater transparency regarding Israeli space activities.

The measure would create a formal system for documenting spacecraft and satellites associated with Israeli operations, alongside the proposed licensing framework.

New space legislation addresses liability, insurance, and damage claims

The drafted law also addresses legal responsibility for damage caused by space activities, including potential accidents involving satellites and other spacecraft.

It would establish a framework for compensating the state for damages or liabilities arising from space operations and introduce provisions allowing insurance requirements to be imposed on operators.

These measures are intended to clarify financial and legal responsibilities in cases involving damage linked to space activities.

The proposed legislation would therefore establish a national framework covering the authorization, registration, supervision, and financial responsibilities of Israeli space operations, both within the country and abroad.
